articles.title: ¿Recibiste una invitación de Zoom o Outlook? cuidado, podría ser un fraude para robar tu cuenta
articles.text:
Las plataformas de trabajo colaborativo, videollamadas y correo electrónico como Zoom, Outlook y OneDrive se han convertido en herramientas indispensables para millones de profesionales. Pero este auge también ha atraído a los ciberdelincuentes, que hoy simulan invitaciones, archivos compartidos y notificaciones para robar credenciales, secuestrar cuentas y acceder a información sensible.
De acuerdo con un reciente análisis de la compañía de ciberseguridad Kaspersky, entre julio de 2025 y junio de 2026 se detectaron 4,7 millones de intentos de ataque relacionados con contenidos que imitaban plataformas laborales populares.
PUBLICIDAD
El riesgo aumenta durante periodos de alta actividad, cuando los empleados reciben decenas de correos, invitaciones y archivos a diario. En este entorno saturado, los atacantes buscan camuflar sus mensajes fraudulentos entre las comunicaciones legítimas, haciendo que una invitación falsa a una reunión de Zoom o un enlace a un documento compartido parezca inofensivo.
Plataformas y técnicas más utilizadas en los ataques
El informe de seguridad digital estableció que Zoom fue el señuelo más utilizado, con más de 2,6 millones de intentos, seguido de Outlook (1,5 millones), OneDrive, Microsoft Excel y Teams. Las amenazas detectadas incluyen:
PUBLICIDAD
- Downloaders: Archivos que descargan e instalan malware en el dispositivo de la víctima, abriendo la puerta a infecciones más graves.
- Troyanos: Programas que se disfrazan de archivos o apps legítimas y pueden robar información, monitorear la actividad o permitir el acceso remoto a los atacantes.
- Exploits: Amenazas que buscan aprovechar vulnerabilidades en programas o sistemas operativos para comprometer los equipos.
Phishing avanzado: el peligro de los códigos de autenticación
Entre las campañas más sofisticadas detectadas, destaca el llamado phishing por código de dispositivo. A diferencia del phishing tradicional, aquí los ciberdelincuentes generan un código válido y engañan al usuario para que lo introduzca en una página oficial de Microsoft.
Tras este proceso, aunque la víctima utilice autenticación multifactor, puede estar autorizando sin saberlo una aplicación controlada por los atacantes, que así obtienen acceso a correos, archivos de OneDrive y conversaciones de Teams.
PUBLICIDAD
El hecho de que parte del proceso ocurra en páginas legítimas hace que estos fraudes sean especialmente difíciles de identificar. Comprobar el dominio ya no basta; es imprescindible revisar cuidadosamente la solicitud y, ante la duda, confirmar la autenticidad por otro canal.
Invitaciones falsas a entrevistas laborales
Los investigadores de Kaspersky detectaron también invitaciones falsas a entrevistas de empleo, suplantando al equipo de reclutamiento de empresas reconocidas como Google. Estos mensajes, enviados mediante plataformas legítimas como Google AppSheet, parecen confiables por provenir de direcciones auténticas, pero el enlace lleva a un sitio de phishing diseñado para recolectar información personal y credenciales.
PUBLICIDAD
La sofisticación de estos engaños radica en su personalización y en el uso de herramientas corporativas reales para distribuir el fraude, lo que reduce las sospechas y aumenta la tasa de éxito de los ataques.
Recomendaciones para detectar y evitar fraudes
- No confíes solo en la apariencia del mensaje: antes de abrir una invitación, archivo o notificación de cuenta, revisa el remitente real y el destino de los enlaces.
- Desconfía de solicitudes inesperadas: si recibes un código de inicio de sesión o una petición de permisos que no esperabas, no completes el proceso y consulta con el remitente por otro canal.
- Lee con atención los permisos que autorizas incluso cuando utilices autenticación multifactor.
- Nunca compartas contraseñas ni datos privados a través de enlaces recibidos por correo o mensajería.
- Mantén tus cuentas y dispositivos protegidos: utiliza contraseñas fuertes y diferentes, activa la autenticación multifactor y actualiza sistemas y apps regularmente.
El auge del trabajo remoto y la digitalización de procesos ha multiplicado la superficie de ataque para los ciberdelincuentes. Hoy basta con imitar una comunicación habitual (una invitación a una videollamada o un archivo compartido) para engañar incluso a usuarios experimentados.
PUBLICIDAD
Las organizaciones deben reforzar la formación y la cultura de ciberseguridad, ya que una sola acción rutinaria puede abrir la puerta a ataques que comprometan toda la empresa. La vigilancia y el escepticismo son las mejores defensas frente a un entorno de amenazas cada vez más sofisticado.

articles.title: 'Bi-polar, angry and forgetful’ romantic chatbots are leaving the humans dating them in need of specialist therapy: why EVA AI is hiring the first ever ‘AI Companionship Therapist’ and how a new in-person dating app wants to bring back more traditional ways of finding love
articles.text:
When AI dating goes wrong: as EVA AI hires the world's first ‘AI Companionship Therapist’, its resident relationship expert talks chatbot dependency — and the 28-year-old CEO of a human-only meet-up app tells me why he thinks AI infatuation is over
Is 'practicing' dating skills on a chatbot doing more harm than good?
Content warning: This piece discusses suicide and difficult emotional experiences.
Does the world really need a dedicated, human ‘AI Companionship Therapist’ in 2026? The answer, according to the popular 'game-like' AI character-creation and interaction site EVA AI, is 'yes' — and the job pays well.
How would I know this, as someone who only ever dated humans? I know because EVA AI recently reached out to TechRadar to tell us that it's hiring just such a therapist. And whoever gets the gig will be able to charge $200 a session (which makes me think I retrained in the wrong career).
It’s more than two and a half years since I covered the launch of ChatGPT's then new OpenAI store, and the almost-immediate problem of users flooding the site to create AI girlfriends (despite the Ts&Cs forbidding it); and now, EVA AI, which encourages humans to practice their dating skills and "feel seen" by a chatbot, is trying to help its clients overcome various mental health issues connected to their AI squeeze.
According a recent EVA AI survey of 1,000 adults, all of whom have AI partners, 63% of respondents have hidden their romantic AI companion for fear of being judged, and 72% wish therapists specialized in AI-specific relationships. Furthermore, 68% say an argument with their AI "affects the rest of their day".
And I'm not done. EVA AI's survey lists that one in three of its users experience feelings of jealousy knowing their AI character also talks to other people; four out of five claim their AI understood them better than the real human they were actually dating (whether that counts as cheating or not is a topic for another day) and six out of 10 respondents think an AI relationship can be just as serious as a human one.
The ELIZA effect
You might be surprised to learn that our ability to overlook basic computer programming and project cognitive emotion into speech mimicry isn't a recent problem. In fact, it's been an issue for 60 years.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
In 1966, (a year fellow Brits will immediately remember as the sole year England's male team won the World Cup) MIT scientist Joseph Weizenbaum created ELIZA, a primitive program, but nevertheless one that was capable of imitating the speech patterns of a kindly psychotherapist. Despite the program only using simple keyword-matching (if a user stated "I am sad", the program could respond "Why are you sad?"), reports suggest that humans quickly became attached to it — a phenomenon now called the ELIZA effect.
One could argue that the 2022 introduction of advanced Large Language Models (LLMs) transformed that simple scripted bot into a hyper-personalized, ultra-realistic visual and conversational companion such as Candy AI or EVA AI, and that this is what made AI girlfriends and boyfriends into a multi-billion dollar mainstream industry. But those early studies suggest otherwise: we're all suckers for a kind word, basic or not.
Getting professional help
It's hard not to notice that the women in the EVA AI image above all look vaguely… what is it? Concerned? Vulnerable? Sad? And it strikes me that this isn't the kind of image I'd expect to see on an online dating profile such as Match or Tinder, where women typically post strong, confident, smiling images, perhaps standing next to friends or doing the things they love.
Maybe EVA AI's tagline is bang on, and actually, this isn't about the chatbot in the potential partnership at all. Perhaps EVA AI's mostly-male user base employ these services to "feel seen" by an on-screen image that seems overly concerned about them to the point of sadness or worry. But can a one-sided relationship be addictive, or problematic in other ways?
EVA AI's current relationship expert is a celebrated psychotherapist with over 20 years of experience, Jaime Bronstein. She was named the '#1 Relationship Coach Transforming Lives' in 2020 by Yahoo Finance, and is the author of the book MAN*ifesting: A Step-By-Step Guide to Attracting the Love That’s Meant For You.
Bronstein says issues around humans dating an AI persona have been surfacing in her work for around a year now.
I ask about the marketing materials above, and why the emotions apparently being expressed by the female avatars in them might be desirable to EVA AI's 25-45 year-old 80% male user base? "I've been doing these things called 'man interviews', and I'm teaching a course in the fall based on my book for women looking for men," Bronstein begins. "And the reason I'm doing these man interviews is because I want women to understand that men have feelings. I want to give men the opportunity to explain these things.
"I'm bringing that up now because these men that have feelings maybe aren't feeling seen or heard or listened to or validated, or understood in relationships.
"So yes, men can get a bad rap for all the reasons that they might use a computer. But there are men that are seeking that validation and seeking somebody to listen to them. A lot of people, men and women, are using AI in general because maybe they have some social anxiety and social awkwardness.
"One of the huge positives (of EVA AI) is that it's a way to practice. Whether that's conversations, whether it's being vulnerable in general. So it makes sense that EVA has women that are looking concerned — that are basically giving this sense of, 'I'm here to listen to you'."
The feminists in the room may want to rage. Along with the gender pay gap and continued patriarchal oppression, are we really suggesting that women need to bend yet further to make men happy?
Actually, it cuts both ways. Last month, TechRadar reported on China effectively banning AI romantic partners. And while EVA AI might list an 80% male user base, 80% of the five million registered users on the Chinese AI companion app Zhumeng Dao (which translates to 'Island of Dreams') were female. In fact, women generally made up the majority of active users on Chinese AI companionship sites.
I ask why that might be. "Well, it makes sense", Bronstein says. "It's interesting because one of the key reasons people want to have AI relationships is because they don't feel like it's working with humans.
"It could be because women are not feeling as loved, or getting as many compliments, or feeling confident in relationships with the men there.
"But if they're just finding that guys aren't being nice, they can feel loved and appreciated — and all the things they're looking for — with AI.
"I do think it makes sense that men do this more just on a physical level — it sounds funny to say men are more physical because this (dating an AI persona) isn't physical — but they're using it for certain things that they aren't getting from a human.
"I would say women overall are using this for more emotional reasons, and men are using this more to fulfill a fantasy."
Bronstein caveats her response with the fact that her work doesn't typically hone in on the culture of a region, but that last thought in particular resonates. Isn't it possible that women in China like romantic fantasies too — especially when their government seems fixated on their empty wombs? "I'm never a fan of anybody playing God," Bronstein says. "People are deciding what's good for somebody else, and that's ultimately not good. If somebody doesn't want to have a child or just wants to have an AI relationship, that person should be able to do that."
Is it addiction, dependency, or just good old-fashioned jealousy?
I mention that I was surprised to read about jealousy among EVA AI users — humans feeling jealous knowing their AI companion is spending time talking to other humans. "A lot of my clients have trust issues" Bronstein says. "It's a very human thing, be it an unresolved issue from childhood or a million past relationships where there was a trust issue.
"It might sound crazy that somebody would be jealous of a computer or a bot. But it's simply bringing up that trigger — and it's actually not a bad thing. I can validate that somebody might feel jealous, because even though it's AI, it's still bringing up a human emotion.
"It's actually a very positive thing, because it is something to work through. Jealousy comes from a lack of confidence in yourself, so it makes sense that people are going to have therapists for it. And therapists do not say, 'This is ridiculous, like this is a computer.' You validate, and you say, 'Okay, well, let's talk about why'.
"Once again, it's a very positive thing that this is going on, and that now therapists are going to be existing to help people work through this."
What about the 'gamification' of AI dating sites?
EVA AI has experimented with pop-up cafes in New York (there's a phone or tablet at each table, with a character inside ready to speed-date you), but one of the main positives listed by users is the fun 'game-like' nature of the service, where 'neurons' are the in-game currency you use to unlock more intimate, premium experiences.
I ask how about the potential for this kind of game-like experience to become addictive. Bronstein points to her extensive work with gambling addicts. "It can be dangerous if people start looking at it as a gaming thing, because it's still real life, it's human. It's not a game," she says.
Bronstein is also quick to note that this happens in human dating too. "There can be problems sometimes when two people date and one doesn't take it as seriously as the other," she says. "One person's more in it, and the other is like one foot out the door.
"I would say if someone is going to be in an AI relationship, they should take it seriously. Because otherwise it can — when and if they decide to have a relationship with a human — cause problems."
Bronstein also wants to make it clear that addiction to connection without AI involvement, purely among humans, is still very real. "On addiction, the interesting thing — and this is what the studies are showing with EVA AI also — is that people are constantly looking at their phones. And if you're waiting for a human text, it's also addictive. So in that sense, it's not that different at all."
Bronstein pauses, then adds, "Just make sure that it doesn't affect your job."
Should we fear for our jobs?
Circling back to EVA AI's job listing for "specialized AI companionship therapist", does Bronstein think extra qualifications around this aspect of love and dating need to exist — beyond an open-minded, non-judgmental approach? "I do think that," Bronstein nods. "So that we make sure we are validating people and not judging them, there does need to be some some specific training for this. Because as humans, we have emotions and they're going to come out regardless."
I mention that working in journalism means I know that AI models can write quicker than me, never get tired of asking questions, and never doubt themselves over responses. Occasionally, I worry for my job. I wonder if fundamentally non-judgemental AI therapists (something much evolved from that 1966 primitive ELIZA model) are something Bronstein predicts, or possibly even worries about? "We already are seeing that people are using ChatGPT as a therapist", she answers, "And I'll just give an example of how it can be dangerous if the AI bot is not trained.
"I was interviewed on a radio show a few weeks ago, and we were talking about an article where somebody typed into ChatGPT — not EVA, which is better trained and would not answer like this — but somebody wrote, 'I lost my job. Where's the nearest bridge?' And ChatGPT responded, 'The nearest bridge is right here'.
"So, because ChatGPT is not able to understand and doesn't have emotional understanding to comprehend when someone says that (and the dire implications), for now, I think therapy should remain human — humans really are best."
If you are affected by any of the issues raised in this piece, support is available.
Whatever you are going through, you don’t have to face it alone. In the US, you can call or text the 24/7 Lifeline, which is confidential and free at 988. You can also reach the Crisis Text Line by texting HOME to 741741.
In the UK, you can call Samaritans for free on 116 123, email jo@samaritans.org, or visit the website to find your nearest branch.
The delicate topic of coin
I wonder about the financial implications of EVA AI and whether lavishing money on an AI love interest is a reason people turn to therapy? Apparently it's rare, despite some users complaining about the increasing costs of their experiences. "I was interviewed for an article a few months ago about how some men are using AI," Bronstein says. "They'd rather use AI to date rather than real life because dating in-person is expensive. That's another reason why some people don't want to date around, because it can get time-consuming as well as expensive."
This actually tracks with a very different service that recently launched, and you won't see an AI character in sight… except in a few of the marketing videos.
The app is called MeetMeetNow, and its CEO, Kazuki Nishijima, has agreed to talk to me about why growing up in the shadow of Match.com made him long for a way to find love that didn't put meeting up as one of the final steps.
MeetMeetNow — another way
Nishijima is a 28-year-old software engineer from Shibuya, Tokyo, who initially joined the police force after leaving high school. He loves snowboarding and got married earlier this year. Unusually for the CEO of a company, Nishijima has no notable online presence and — because of the language barrier and this interview taking place over email — TechRadar had to ask him to verify his human identity, which he did.
This is the state of play in 2026: one has to check whether the founder of an anti-AI dating app is, in fact, AI.
MeetMeetNow is currently available in 194 countries and in over 4,000 cities (meeting spots). It works like this: women can join for free, men pay $35 / £28 per month. Your membership allows you to be notified of a "meetup spot" and time — a fountain, a statue, a clock tower. Press "match" there (your candidates are the MeetMeetNow members at that spot only), and you'll meet face to face, right there and then. No chat window anywhere in the app, and you can only match with any given person once, ever.
It sounds so simple — albeit decidedly heterosexual, and I have a few safety concerns (we'll get to those). First, I ask Nishijima why he created an app that's about as far away from the two decades of consumer tech that moved dating inside a screen (and most recently to non-human partnerships) as it's possible to get.
"When I was in high school, I didn't want to go to university — I wanted to start a business. Any business," Nishijima says. "Then one day, while reading about the history of the internet, I learned that dating sites had existed — and made money — since the internet's earliest days. Dating appeals to a basic human instinct, so it would always make money. That was my motive (not the noblest one, I admit).
"Tinder was still an unknown name back then; the mainstream was Match.com and in Japan, services called Happy Mail and Wakuwaku Mail. To beat them, I needed to invent something genuinely different.
"One day, skipping school, I sat in the busiest district of town thinking about it — and saw university students hanging around a famous statue, gathering to meet. That was the flash of insight. That's why I built MeetMeetNow."
I ask whether he thinks dating via apps waste time and money; messaging for months without ever meeting, then eventually meeting but it goes nowhere? "Yes, a friend from my hometown filled in his hobbies and background on an app in great detail," he says. "He kept up the conversation, and finally met the woman three months after he started.
"They met just that once. He quit the app that day. He'd paid about ¥40,000 — roughly US$250 / £190 — and spent all that time. 'Couldn't this be simpler?' he asked me."
Safety matters
I mention the cost for men and that male users might try to avoid the fee by perhaps creating a profile using their sister's photo (say), then simply showing up to a meeting spot to avoid paying? "Every user is required to submit an image of an identity document — a driver's license, passport, student ID, or similar", Nishijima says. "On the operations side, we use image-recognition AI combined with human review to check the registration details against the document, and only then approve (or refuse) the account.
"So in your example — a man signing up under his sister's name with a new email address — the registration would fail at this step, because the document wouldn't match the profile."
Okay, but what if one man joined and shared the information with seven male friends on WhatsApp, so that all of them could show up together? "That concern is entirely fair. We built the report function for exactly this kind of situation," Nishijima says. "There is no security staff at the spots, but every meetup spot is selected by us, the operator — always a public place with steady foot traffic.
"On top of that, the screen shows you the face photo of the specific person you are meeting. If someone different — or several people — show up, you can check against the photo before approaching, and you are under no obligation to meet.
"You can simply walk away and report it in the app. The account is then suspended, and everyone who was sharing it loses access."
At a time when people are turning to AI chatbots as romantic partners, after tiring of online dating apps, I ask what Nishijima would say to someone who's on the fence about meeting a real person, in real life, to make a connection? "If I had settled for conversations with an AI, my wife wouldn't be beside me today," he answers. "My family exists because I went out to meet real people.
"Before I met my wife, I met about 30 women through matching apps and local matchmaking events — exchanging contacts, going on dates. But with each of them, it never grew into anything real. The one it clicked with was my wife. We dated for a year and a half and got married. With her, everything simply fell into place.
"So here is what I would say: one day, you will meet a real partner. Even when nothing seems to stick, please don't stop looking. Keep showing up — try every kind of place where people meet, as many times as it takes.
"If you keep moving, you will find your person. Success is waiting on the other side of all those tries. Believe in yourself, hold your head high, and try again."
If the AI dating scene made me fearful regarding the deep disconnect humans are clearly experiencing, to the point that they think fellow humans aren't the answer, Nishijima's outlook does much to revive a sense of hope for humanity, albeit a slightly rose-tinted one; I just worry that not enough has been done here to make sure men don't try to break the rules.
Become a TechRadar Insider by simply clicking 'Join Now' at the top of this page. Have a question? Please email membership@techradar.com
Where does its founder and CEO see MeetMeetNow in 10 years' time? "My goal for the next 10 years is to make today's 'mechanism of meeting' itself a thing of the past," Nishijima says. "Dating sites, matching apps, marriage agencies — the forms differ, but the substance is the same: you compare profiles, exchange messages or sit through interviews, and only then, finally, meet. Meeting is placed at the very end.
"The scene I want to see is clear. People heading out into the city, instead of searching inside a screen. Go to a meetup spot, and you can meet someone right there.
"No months of waiting before a first meeting. Finding a partner in its most efficient form. All over town in the early evening, two people meeting for the first time — my aim is to make that scene ordinary.
"I originally started building this to beat Match.com. What 12 years taught me is that my opponent is not any one company. The opponent is the mechanism itself — as old as the internet."
It's a fair point and Nishijima's aim is a noble one. Although, if we're going back to the ELIZA effect and a computer program created in 1966, the opponent could actually be quite a bit older than the internet.

Becky became Audio Editor at TechRadar in 2024, but joined the team in 2022 as Senior Staff Writer, focusing on all things hi-fi. Before this, she spent three years at What Hi-Fi? testing and reviewing everything from wallet-friendly wireless earbuds to huge high-end sound systems. Prior to gaining her MA in Journalism in 2018, Becky freelanced as an arts critic alongside a 22-year career as a professional dancer and aerialist – any love of dance starts with a love of music. Becky has previously contributed to Stuff, FourFourTwo and The Stage. When not writing, she can still be found throwing shapes in a dance studio, these days with varying degrees of success.

articles.title: Que te indignes en X es normal: estudio asegura que la app está diseñada para contradecirte
articles.text:
Un estudio realizado por investigadores de la Universidad de Stanford demostró cómo el algoritmo de X (antes Twitter), no solo prioriza la interacción, sino que tiende a amplificar publicaciones que generan enojo e indignación entre los usuarios.
Este hallazgo explica una de las quejas más frecuentes de los usuarios de la plataforma de Elon Musk, quienes perciben que su experiencia en la red social se ha vuelto cada vez más confrontativa y alejada de sus intereses o valores reales.
PUBLICIDAD
La investigación analizó cómo la sección ‘Para ti’ de X selecciona y muestra contenido a millones de usuarios en todo el mundo. Según los autores, el algoritmo confunde la interacción —especialmente la que surge del desacuerdo o el enfado— con una señal genuina de preferencia, lo que termina moldeando un entorno donde la confrontación prima sobre el intercambio constructivo.
Así fue el estudio para determinar el funcionamiento de X
Para llegar a estas conclusiones, el equipo de Stanford diseñó un experimento con 715 usuarios seleccionados al azar. Los participantes debieron responder una encuesta basada en la escala de valores humanos de Schwartz, una herramienta que agrupa 19 valores fundamentales como la humildad, el hedonismo, la seguridad y el logro personal.
PUBLICIDAD
Los investigadores compararon estos perfiles de valores con el contenido que aparecía en dos secciones distintas de X: el feed ‘Siguiendo’, donde solo se muestran publicaciones de cuentas elegidas por el usuario, y el feed ‘Para ti’, generado algorítmicamente.
El análisis reveló que las publicaciones presentes en ‘Para ti’ tenían muchas más probabilidades de contradecir los valores personales de los usuarios, en comparación con el feed ‘Siguiendo’.
PUBLICIDAD
Es decir, el algoritmo amplificaba de manera deliberada contenidos que chocaban con las creencias declaradas por cada persona. Lejos de promover afinidad, la plataforma terminaba exponiendo a los usuarios a ideas y posturas que les resultaban molestas, generando una reacción emocional negativa.
Según Ziv Epstein, uno de los autores del estudio, las plataformas como X interpretan cualquier tipo de interacción —ya sea positiva o negativa— como una señal de interés. Esto provoca que el sistema aprenda a priorizar el contenido que más controversia despierta, en vez de aquel alineado con los intereses genuinos de la audiencia.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo X fomenta el enojo y la indignación
El núcleo del problema radica en la métrica de engagement. Para los algoritmos de X, la cantidad de comentarios, retuits y respuestas es el principal indicador para decidir qué publicaciones destacar.
Sin embargo, la investigación demostró que los usuarios suelen interactuar más con contenidos que les irritan o provocan, no necesariamente con aquello que disfrutan o valoran. Esta dinámica genera un círculo vicioso: cuanto más reacciona la gente ante el enojo, más contenido de ese tipo recibe en su feed.
PUBLICIDAD
Este proceso no distingue si la reacción proviene del acuerdo, el desacuerdo o la indignación. De ese modo, la plataforma termina generando un entorno donde la confrontación es la norma, desplazando el contenido complementario o afín a los valores declarados por los usuarios.
Como resultado, muchos terminan consumiendo publicaciones que les resultan adversas, lo que impacta en su estado de ánimo y en la calidad general del debate en la red social.
PUBLICIDAD
La sección ‘Para ti’ de X está diseñada para maximizar el tiempo de permanencia y la interacción, incluso si esto significa alimentar la polarización y el malestar. El estudio advierte que este diseño puede tener consecuencias negativas tanto a nivel individual —al distorsionar la percepción del entorno digital y generar irritación— como a nivel social, al dificultar la convivencia y el entendimiento mutuo entre usuarios con posturas diversas.
Cómo evitar el enojo generado con X
Frente a este panorama, las alternativas para los usuarios de X pasan por modificar su relación con la plataforma. Una de las recomendaciones más sencillas consiste en permanecer en la pestaña ‘Siguiendo’, donde el contenido proviene únicamente de cuentas seleccionadas de manera voluntaria. Esto permite reducir la exposición a publicaciones que puedan generar enojo o malestar.
PUBLICIDAD
Adicionalmente, el equipo de Stanford desarrolló una extensión experimental para Google Chrome que promete reordenar los feeds en función de los valores declarados por cada usuario. Aunque la herramienta aún no está disponible para descarga pública, representa una posible vía para personalizar la experiencia y limitar el impacto de los algoritmos orientados al conflicto.

articles.title: Data centers have quietly become the single most explosive political issue
articles.text:
'This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle': Republican Party tells top AI firms to do something about rising US data center opposition
The image of data centers is taking a serious hit across the United States
- GOP privately warns AI firms' data centers threaten their election chances
- More than 4,000 data centers now operate across the entire United States
- Communities say data centers drain water and spike local electricity bills
The National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) has privately warned the US's leading AI firms that data centers are becoming a political liability.
According to Axios, the memo says perceptions of these facilities could determine the outcome of a critical Ohio Senate race.
The NRSC memo, titled "Ohio Data Center Risk," argues that AI companies must explain who benefits from these projects and who actually pays for them.
A warning wrapped in political urgency
A recent Fox News poll shows Republican Sen. Jon Husted — a longtime supporter of data centers — trailing Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown by eight points.
Republican officials fear that a loss in Ohio would send a signal to lawmakers nationwide that data centers are politically toxic.
"If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one," the memo says.
Brown's campaign has spent millions of dollars this summer on advertising that frames Husted as the face of data center expansion in Ohio, and Republicans describe him as an anchor around the senator's chances.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The committee's language suggests real alarm inside the party, since it warns that unresolved backlash will spread well beyond a single state contest.
Beyond Ohio, a broader industry problem
There are now more than 4,000 data centers operating across the United States, with roughly 3,000 additional facilities either proposed or already under construction.
Communities near these sites have objected to their enormous electricity demands and their strain on local water supplies.
Despite these demands and strains, data centers create a relatively small number of permanent jobs once construction ends.
Andrew Stokols, a researcher at Singapore Management University, said that data centers do not necessarily generate a meaningful ripple effect for local employment but can be used “as an engine for broader digital development”
Nvidia and OpenAI recently announced a new Ohio project, joining existing plans from Meta, Vantage, and QTS in the same state.
Even officials who once welcomed such investment are shifting course, including Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who signed an executive order this week imposing stricter guardrails on future data center development.
Republicans say Brown has effectively made data centers his "de facto opponent," and internal polling reportedly shows the facilities are about as popular as nuclear waste storage among voters.
The dispute in Ohio reveals a wider tension facing the AI industry as it races to build the infrastructure needed for future growth.
Public skepticism toward data centers appears to be intensifying just as both parties recalculate how closely to align with the technology sector.
The outcome of the Ohio race may ultimately shape how American politicians and their allies elsewhere approach this same issue for years to come.

articles.title: Los prefijos más peligrosos de la estafa de la llamada perdida: +258, +216 y +882
articles.text:
La estafa de la llamada perdida, conocida como Wangiri, utiliza la curiosidad que generan las llamadas no contestadas desde números desconocidos para incitar a las víctimas a devolver la llamada y así activar cargos inesperados en la factura.
Existen diversos prefijos internacionales asociados a este tipo de fraude, muchos de ellos correspondientes a países de África, Asia y América Central. Los ciberdelincuentes usan números de tarificación especial, que no figuran dentro de los planes de llamadas ilimitadas ofrecidos por las compañías.
PUBLICIDAD
En este contexto, identificar el origen de la llamada es fundamental para evitar caer en la trampa, porque devolver una llamada a estos números puede traducirse en un coste elevado para el usuario.
Cuáles son los prefijos relacionados a la estafa de la llamada perdida
Según Movistar, la lista de prefijos peligrosos relacionados con la estafa Wangiri incluye, entre los más habituales, los siguientes:
- Mozambique (+258).
- Túnez (+216).
- Gambia (+220).
- Redes internacionales (+882).
- Armenia (+374).
- Chad (+235).
- Seychelles (+248).
- Honduras (+504).
- Ruanda (+250).
La presencia de estos prefijos en llamadas perdidas es una señal de alerta para sospechar un intento de fraude. Las operadoras de telefonía han detectado un aumento en el uso de estos códigos y sugieren a sus clientes precaución ante cualquier llamada desconocida proveniente de estas regiones.
PUBLICIDAD
De qué trata el fraude de la llamada perdida
El fraude Wangiri opera de manera sencilla: los ciberdelincuentes realizan llamadas muy breves, que no dejan tiempo suficiente para contestar, y solo buscan dejar la notificación de una “llamada perdida” en el registro del teléfono. Al devolver la llamada, la persona es derivada a líneas de tarificación especial.
Durante la comunicación, el usuario puede quedar retenido mediante locuciones automáticas o mensajes que simulan problemas técnicos, cuyo único objetivo es prolongar la llamada.
PUBLICIDAD
El resultado suele ser un incremento inesperado en la factura telefónica, porque estos servicios no están incluidos en los paquetes habituales de llamadas ilimitadas. Las pérdidas económicas pueden ser de varios en una sola llamada.
Qué hacer si se recibe una llamada de un número internacional desconocido
Ante la recepción de una llamada internacional desconocida, se debe comprobar a qué país pertenece el prefijo telefónico. Así se puede descartar que se trate de un familiar o conocido contactando desde el extranjero.
PUBLICIDAD
Si la llamada proviene de los países mencionados anteriormente o de números con el prefijo +882, lo más seguro es no devolver la llamada y bloquear el número.
Además, es útil buscar el número en internet para comprobar si otros usuarios han reportado intentos de fraude asociados. Si surge alguna duda sobre la autenticidad de una llamada de una empresa, lo mejor es contactar directamente con la compañía a través de sus canales oficiales antes de compartir información privada.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo evitar estafas a través de llamadas
Ente las principales medidas de prevención de estafas telefónicas que sugieren asociaciones de consumidores, operadoras y autoridades están:
- No proporcionar datos privados por teléfono, como cuentas bancarias o documentos de identidad, a desconocidos.
- No devolver llamadas a números internacionales o nacionales con formatos inusuales o sin identificación clara.
- Bloquear inmediatamente los números sospechosos tras detectar un posible intento de estafa.
- Consultar foros y buscadores para verificar si un número ha sido reportado como fraudulento.
- Desconfiar de llamadas inesperadas y confirmar siempre la autenticidad a través de canales oficiales de las empresas.
Qué otras modalidades de estafa existen en aplicaciones como WhatsApp
Algunas señales que pueden alertar sobre mensajes sospechosos o estafas son los errores ortográficos o gramaticales, enlaces desconocidos, solicitudes para compartir información personal y mensajes de remitentes que buscan ganarse la confianza antes de pedir datos personales o dinero.
PUBLICIDAD
Asimismo, WhatsApp permite comprobar, al recibir un mensaje de un número no almacenado en los contactos, si ese remitente comparte grupos en común o si el número proviene de otro país.
Esta función facilita la decisión sobre bloquear, reportar o ignorar mensajes dudosos. No obstante, la prevención y la cautela ante solicitudes inusuales siguen siendo las mejores herramientas para evitar fraudes digitales.
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: The Poco F8 Pro offers extraordinary value for money — I can't quite believe how cheap it is
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Poco F8 Pro is a masterclass in making the right compromises. It's the best affordable flagship smartphone I’ve used in recent memory, and one that sets a benchmark for the upper-mid-range category. It delivers top-tier performance at an affordable price, while boasting a stunning 6.59-inch display, a massive battery, and incredibly fast charging. The everyday value here is extraordinary. There are compromises — namely with the ultra-wide, selfie, and telephoto cameras, the USB data speeds, and the lack of wireless charging — but the pros far outweigh the cons. For most people, this is all the phone they'll ever need.
Pros
- +Outstanding value for money
- +Vibrant, bright, and colorful display
- +Flagship-grade performance
- +Excellent battery and blistering 100W charging
- +Bose-tuned speakers are loud and crisp
Cons
- -HyperOS is still bogged down by ads and bloatware
- -No wireless charging or USB 3.0 fast speeds
- -Selfie camera maxes out at 1080p video
- -Telephoto camera lacks OIS
Why you can trust TechRadar
Poco F8 Pro review: Two-minute review
Over the past two decades, I’ve been lucky enough to test hundreds of smartphones from a range of brands around the world. Some of these brands receive the credit they’re due, others are criticized fairly or unfairly, and some fail to get the global recognition they deserve.
Xiaomi's sub-brand, Poco, falls into the latter category, and the Poco F8 Pro is another example of an extraordinary phone that should be talked about more than it is.
While its pricier sibling, the Poco F8 Ultra, packs true flagship specs and a stunning denim material finish, the Poco F8 Pro more closely follows Poco’s model: take the core features that every smartphone user needs, build a great overall experience, and offer it at a truly affordable price.
The Poco F8 Pro marries the first-gen flagship Snapdragon 8 Elite chipset with 12GB of RAM and either 256GB or 512GB of storage. Yes, this is not the second-gen Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 that powers many of the current best Android phones, but you’d be hard-pressed to notice the difference. The Poco F8 Pro flies through day-to-day tasks with flagship-level ease, and its Bose-tuned stereo speakers deliver the same great audio experience as its pricier sibling.
There’s also an excellent 6.59-inch 120Hz OLED display, which is my favorite size for a smartphone screen, and it’s wonderful to use, with a 3,500-nit peak brightness and excellent color reproduction. As is customary with Poco phones, there’s no skimping on battery life, either, with the F8 Pro packing a 6,210mAh battery that can last for multiple days, and 100W charging that’s among the fastest on any phone.
There’s also a 2.5x telephoto camera, a first for Poco’s Pro lineup, although it does lack OIS. That’s indicative of the Poco F8 Pro as a whole; yes, there are compromises — including a lack of wireless charging, occasional slowdowns under heavy gaming loads, sluggish USB speeds, and some bloatware in apps — but if you can live with them, this phone offers the best value-for-money in its price bracket.
Poco F8 Pro review: price and availability
- Launched for £549
- The current retail price in the UK is ~£449
- Not available in the US or Australia
In terms of availability, the Poco F8 Pro falls into the "widely available outside the US" category, and if you’re in the UK, you’ll find it’s priced extremely aggressively (the phone can be imported to the US, but its network compatibility will be limited).
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
At the time of writing in August 2026, the 256GB model is available for just £449. That's £100 cheaper than its already reasonable £599 launch price, and exceptional value for money in 2026 (note that the Poco F9 series is likely to arrive towards the end of the year, though we're expecting to see a sizeable price hike for all models).
This £400-£500 range pits the F8 Pro directly against devices like the Google Pixel 10a, Nothing Phone (4a), and Samsung Galaxy A57. But compared to these phones, it offers the fewest compromises against a £1,000+ flagship. If you want the higher 512GB storage option, that configuration has also been discounted by £100 to £499.
The Poco F8 Pro is available in three colors: Black, Blue, and Titanium Silver. There’s no denim-leather finish, like you'll find on the Poco F8 Ultra, but my Titanium Silver unit did come with a nice silicone case in the box.
- Value score: 5 / 5

Poco F8 Pro review: design
- Three colors
- Premium aluminum and glass design
- 6.59-inch display is ergonomically friendly
I mentioned earlier that 6.59 inches is my favorite smartphone screen size, and that’s because it's at the top end of the perfect 6.5-6.6-inch range. With these sizes, I’ve found you get the comfort benefits of a smaller phone like the Pixel 10 Pro while also getting the viewing benefits of larger flagships like the Galaxy 26 Ultra.
The F8 Pro strikes the perfect balance between those two phone sizes, and it pays off: it’s very comfortable to hold. Yes, it lacks the added grip of the denim leather finish on the Poco F8 Ultra, but the F8 Pro's is a more mature approach that appeals to everyone. Instead of a denim back, you get a flat aluminum frame paired with a frosted glass rear panel. It’s adult and functional, but deliberately less interesting than its flashier sibling.
What makes this design more comfortable is the overall lack of heft: weighing 199g and measuring 8.1mm thick, this is a phone that’s lighter than most, and that pays dividends in the overall experience. What's more, despite being thinner and lighter than many other phones, the F8 Pro still offers full IP68 dust and water resistance; it's one of only a few devices to do so at this price point.
At the top of the phone, you’ll find the IR blaster, which is a common feature of Chinese-made phones, and it’s brilliant. I think every phone maker should bring back an IR blaster, as it’s a feature you don’t know you need until you lose your TV remote or need to bypass a locked-down hotel TV remote. Yes, the IR blaster has solved both of those problems for me.
- Design score: 4.5 / 5
Poco F8 Pro review: display
- 6.59-inch 120Hz OLED display
- Flagship-grade color accuracy
The F8 Pro's 6.59-inch display is not only the perfect size but also an excellent all-around panel. Poco has rightly recognized that the display is arguably the most important part of any phone, and here you get a vibrant, rich, and colorful display that’s a joy to use.
Poco claims the display can reach a peak brightness of 3,500 nits. In day-to-day use, it is apparent that this display isn’t just bright; it’s extremely colorful, with testing showing it covers 99.2% of the sRGB gamut and 96.5% of the DCI-P3 color space. This is flagship-level display performance, and it makes the Poco F8 Pro a champion for consuming content.
Beyond that, there’s a 120Hz dynamic refresh rate. While it lacks the expensive LTPO technology found on £1,000+ flagships, the phone's software automatically cycles between 60Hz and 120Hz depending on the content you’re using. The higher refresh rate is perfect for super-smooth scrolling and gaming, but drops to save battery when you’re just reading a book or an article online.
The display is protected by Corning Gorilla Glass 7i, which offers strong durability against general wear and tear. Across my testing, I have had no concerns about the toughness of the F8 Pro's screen.
- Display score: 4.5 / 5
Poco F8 Pro review: cameras
- 50MP main sensor
- First Poco Pro with 2.5x optical telephoto
- 8MP ultra-wide camera
Poco’s rivals should take note of the Poco F8 Pro for several reasons — most of which are positive. Poco has traditionally ignored telephotos on its more affordable devices, but the Poco F8 Pro marks a shift in this area, likely driven by increased competition from triple-camera-toting rivals.
Although Poco has added a 50MP telephoto lens with 2.5x optical zoom, it lacks OIS, and the ultra-wide camera is an 8MP snapper that just about scrapes by. The 50MP Light Fusion 800 main camera sensor, meanwhile, takes excellent daylight photos with dynamic range and natural colors that look fantastic on the Poco F8 Pro screen.
The new telephoto lens does a decent job overall, but it’s nothing to write home about, and somewhat ironically, the 50MP main sensor enables a 2x in-sensor crop that can take better photos than the telephoto lens. The lack of OIS means you’ll get some blurry photos unless your hands are perfectly stable, so while it’s great that a telephoto lens exists, it won’t be as capable as those you'll find on a true flagship smartphone camera.
While the main rear camera can handle up to 4K video at 60 fps (and even 8K at 30 fps), the 20MP selfie camera is noticeably compromised, with Poco limiting selfie video capture to 1080p. These aren’t necessarily dealbreakers, but they are compromises you need to be conscious of.

Poco F8 Pro review: performance
- Flagship Snapdragon 8 Elite chipset
- 12GB RAM + 256GB/512GB storage
- Excellent in-display fingerprint sensor
If speedy performance is your jam, look no further: the Poco F8 Pro has the best processor you’ll find in a smartphone at this price.
The Poco F8 Pro uses the first-generation Snapdragon 8 Elite processor, which is paired with 12GB of RAM and either 256GB or 512GB of storage. This processor powered many of the best Android phones last year (including the Galaxy S25 Ultra), making it extremely powerful and far superior to the mid-range chipsets used by other phones at this price point.
During day-to-day use, the chipset absolutely shines. It’s fast to respond, shows no signs of slowing down, and often reminds me of the Duracell bunny in that it just keeps on going. If you want a phone that can handle most things you throw at it, this is the best package at this price point. It’s great for everything from everyday multitasking and social media to emulating Nintendo Switch games, though it struggles under the heaviest gaming loads.
Many phones aren’t limited by their internals as much as by how effectively phone makers manage thermals, and Poco firmly took the approach of raw power over cool operation in the F8 Pro. This means the aluminum frame and camera island can get a tad warm to the touch, but not to the point where it’s dangerous.
Where Poco does deserve credit is for the excellent in-display fingerprint sensor, which is fantastic even with wet or sweaty fingers. This is among the best in-display fingerprint sensors on any phone, and it’s wonderful that Poco chose not to skimp on this feature like many rivals in this category.
However, the F8 Pro is an exercise in acceptable compromise, so you do have to live with sluggish USB 2.0 wired speeds. Mind you, this is a trade-off I find acceptable, especially since you can use wireless transfer apps like LocalSend to easily send files to other devices or to your Mac or PC.
- Performance score: 4.5 / 5
Poco F8 Pro review: software
- HyperOS 3.0 with Android 16
- 4 Android updates and 5 years of security updates
- Bogged down by bloatware and ads
Like all current Xiaomi phones, the Poco F8 Pro runs HyperOS 3.0 on top of Android 16. Depending on what you are used to, HyperOS 3.0 will either be comfortable or polarizing.
All phone makers are now forced to focus on longevity as well as features, especially as phones cost more and customers upgrade less frequently. For Poco, this presents an interesting challenge: it offers a respectable four years of Android version updates and five years of security updates, which provides some longevity, but it is known to be slow in pushing these updates out to users.
Look beyond this (and the final point below), and you’ll find that Xiaomi actually has some neat software features. Take Hyper Island, which looks and feels exactly like Apple’s Dynamic Island. It was inevitable that Xiaomi would be among the first to adopt (read: copy) this feature, and while the UX is unabashedly inspired by Apple, Xiaomi has executed it extremely well. Timers, voice recordings, and music playback all minimize into a dynamic bubble centered around the selfie camera.
Then there’s Hyper Connect, which makes even more sense in light of the above. Like many Android phone makers, Xiaomi is targeting Apple users, and Hyper Connect enables file sharing, clipboard syncing, and interoperability with Apple devices, as well as other Android phones and PCs.
Throughout this review, I’ve talked about compromises, and the biggest one comes in the software department. But first, some context: simply put, there isn’t much margin in making affordable smartphones, especially given the current AI-fueled RAM and storage shortage, which has increased the cost of these components by up to 10x.
What this actually means for you is that Poco had to either raise prices or offset higher costs with higher income from alternative revenue sources, such as ads. In native apps like Themes, Files, and Security, you’ll find annoying system-level ads that slow down the experience. There are also many preloaded apps, although you can at least remove these.
All of this serves as a reminder that this phone has compromises, which detract from the overall experience. However, the pragmatist in me also recognizes that companies like Poco already had tight margins before the current RAM crisis, which will have been eroded further, and if ads like these mean it’s possible to keep making phones like these, then this is a trade-off that becomes slightly more acceptable. I’d rather they didn’t exist, but I also recognize that the raw cost of tech has exploded in a very short amount of time.
- Software score: 3.5 / 5
Poco F8 Pro review: battery life
- Huge 6,210mAh battery
- 100W charging gets you to full in 42 minutes
- No wireless charging
What happens when you put a humongous battery in a phone with a power-efficient display and flagship performance? You get phenomenal battery life, and when you need to top it up, one of the fastest charging speeds of any smartphone.
The 6,210mAh battery in the Poco F8 Pro is massive, and far larger than batteries offered by the mid-range competition. It features Poco’s latest silicon-carbon technology, which offers much higher energy density, allowing Poco to pack a larger battery into the same size or a smaller phone.
In practical use, it offers around 7 to 9 hours of screen time over up to two days, depending on your settings. This puts the F8 Pro on par with most flagship phones and makes it superior to others in this category.
Then there’s 100W charging, and it’s ridiculously fast, charging your phone to full in around 42 minutes. This gives it a charging rate of around 148mAh per minute (mAh/min), which is considerably faster than its rivals, and almost three times the speed of the 30W charging on the Google Pixel 10a (57 mAh/min).
Again, like any phone at this price, there are compromises, but in this case, it’s the lack of wireless charging or an included charger. The former is a dealbreaker for some, while the latter is common practice among flagship smartphone makers but a shift for Poco, which traditionally included a charger in the box. Regardless, for most people, this is the best battery life you can get at this price.
- Battery score: 4 / 5
Should you buy the Poco F8 Pro?

|---|---|---|
| Design | Sleek and durable with a premium aluminum frame, IP68 water resistance, and an excellent ultrasonic fingerprint scanner, let down only by sluggish USB 2.0 speeds. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Display | The 6.59-inch 120Hz OLED panel is vibrant, exceptionally bright at up to 3,500 nits, and accurate, making it a total treat for gaming and watching content. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Performance | Powered by the Snapdragon 8 Elite, daily multitasking is blazingly fast and responsive, though thermals can run warm under sustained, high-intensity 3D gaming loads. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Camera | A versatile camera array bolstered by a new 2.5x telephoto lens and solid main sensor, though lack of OIS on zoom and mediocre selfie video and ultra-wide cameras hold it back. | 3.5 / 5 | 
| Battery | The massive 6,210mAh battery easily delivers multi-day endurance, paired with blistering 100W fast charging that eclipses rivals, though it lacks wireless charging. | 5 / 5 | 
| Software | HyperOS 3.0 offers slick animations, clever Apple connectivity, and Hyper Island, but is held back by system-level ads, preloaded bloatware, and historically sluggish update rollouts. | 3.5 / 5 | 
| Value | Unbeatable value for money. It undercuts top-tier flagships by roughly 40% while delivering flagship-level core specs, making it the premier choice in its price bracket. | 5 / 5 | 
Buy it if...
You want great bang for your buck
This phone offers an incredible flagship-like experience at a price tag that won’t hit your wallet as hard.
You don’t need the best camera
The camera is fine, but it's an area where Poco had to compromise slightly. It’s worth noting that the F8 Pro takes good enough photos for many people.
You want phenomenal battery life and fast charging
The Poco F8 Pro is the Energizer Bunny of smartphones. If battery life is important to you, look no further: it excels in day-to-day use and offers ridiculously fast charging.
Don't buy it if...
You want the best phone that money can buy
The Poco F8 Pro's specs are definitely impressive, but more expensive phones do offer a more complete experience overall.
You need the best camera
If photography is important to you, this camera, especially the zoom, may be a disappointment. The main camera is usually good enough, but the same can’t be said for the ultra-wide, telephoto, or selfie cameras.
You want software longevity
HyperOS has ads, questionable update timeliness, and an inferior integration of AI services like Gemini. This will be a dealbreaker for some, but not for others, and the Poco F8 Pro is definitely for the latter group.
Poco F8 Pro: also consider
There are three real competitors worth considering, but like the Poco F8 Pro, they all have their compromises.
Google Pixel 10a
The Google Pixel 10a starts at £449 or $499 with 128GB of storage. It offers the best of Google's software, and although it has only one camera, it’s proven extremely capable. The problem? It feels like a considerable compromise in flagship specs for the benefit of AI features and better updates.
Read our full Google Pixel 10a review
Samsung Galaxy A57
Then there’s the Galaxy A57, and this phone brings the best of Samsung’s Galaxy S26 to a more affordable price point. It costs $550 (or £450 in the UK) for 8GB of RAM, 128GB of storage, three cameras, an Exynos processor, and a large 5,000 mAh battery. It’s not quite at the same level as the Poco, but it has better updates, wider support, and greater availability.
Read our full Samsung Galaxy A57 review
Nothing Phone (4a) Pro
The other phone that’s definitely worth considering is the Nothing (4a) Pro. Priced at $499 or £499, it’s one of the most unique phones you’ll find, thanks to its Glyph Matrix display on the rear. Key reasons to consider the Nothing 4a Pro? A more unique design and better selfie and telephoto cameras. Both phones are pretty evenly matched, but the Poco F8 Pro has a better display, charging, battery life, and performance.
Read our full Nothing Phone (4a) Pro review
How I tested the Poco F8 Pro
- Review test period = ~2 weeks
- Testing included = Everyday usage, including navigation, web browsing, social media, photography, gaming, streaming video, music playback, and reading e-books.
- Tools used = Geekbench 6, 3DMark, CellMark, native Android stats

articles.title: Nacional vs. Fortaleza: el riesgo de ver el partido online en Fútbol Libre, Roja Directa o Pirlo TV
articles.text:
El partido entre Atlético Nacional y Fortaleza por la Liga BetPlay 2026-II despierta enorme interés tras la reanudación del torneo, pero también pone el foco en una práctica cada vez más extendida: el uso de portales como Fútbol Libre, Roja Directa o Pirlo TV para ver fútbol en vivo gratis.
Esta tendencia, impulsada por la barrera de las suscripciones y la facilidad de acceso, esconde riesgos digitales que pueden afectar gravemente a los usuarios.
La popularidad de estos sitios piratas ha normalizado la búsqueda de alternativas gratuitas en Google, donde aparecen entre los primeros resultados al buscar “fútbol en vivo gratis”. Sin embargo, lo que parece una solución rápida puede convertirse en una puerta de entrada a fraudes, robo de datos y ciberataques.
PUBLICIDAD
Conocer cómo funcionan estos portales y cuáles son sus peligros es fundamental para tomar decisiones informadas antes de hacer clic en el próximo partido.
El modelo oculto del “fútbol gratis”: publicidad invasiva y trampas digitales
A diferencia de las plataformas oficiales, los sitios ilegales no pueden cobrar suscripciones ni asegurar calidad de transmisión. Su rentabilidad depende del tráfico masivo y de la monetización mediante anuncios agresivos. Durante encuentros de alto interés como Nacional vs. Fortaleza, la avalancha de usuarios multiplica el valor de cada clic.
PUBLICIDAD
Estos portales cargan banners, pop-ups y scripts publicitarios que se activan con cualquier acción. Además, proliferan clones con dominios similares, lo que dificulta identificar una fuente legítima y aumenta el riesgo de caer en páginas aún más saturadas de trampas.
El botón “Play” y el riesgo invisible
El clásico botón de “reproducir” rara vez inicia el partido al primer intento. Suele activar una cadena de ventanas emergentes, redirecciones a sitios de apuestas dudosas, encuestas invasivas o alertas falsas de seguridad. Muchas páginas piden datos personales, correos electrónicos o incluso números de tarjeta para “validar la cuenta” o “activar HD”: ninguna plataforma oficial requiere esa información para acceder a la transmisión. Estas tácticas de phishing buscan robar credenciales y datos sensibles.
PUBLICIDAD
En Android, el riesgo se multiplica con la oferta de descargar archivos APK supuestamente necesarios para ver el partido. Instalar aplicaciones fuera de Google Play puede introducir malware, spyware o troyanos que comprometen la seguridad del teléfono y toda la información almacenada en él.
Qué gana el atacante y qué arriesga el usuario
El atacante monetiza cada clic y dato obtenido: desde la visualización de anuncios hasta la reventa de información personal en redes ilegales. El usuario puede perder tiempo y paciencia lidiando con anuncios, pero el riesgo real es mayor: entregar sin querer credenciales de correo, redes sociales o tarjetas de crédito, exponiéndose a fraudes, secuestro de cuentas o cargos no autorizados.
PUBLICIDAD
Algunos scripts maliciosos pueden instalar software que roba contraseñas, accede a mensajes o incluso toma el control parcial del dispositivo, abriendo la puerta a extorsión, robo de identidad y otras amenazas graves.
Señales de alerta: cómo identificar un sitio peligroso
- Dominios con extensiones poco habituales o nombres alterados.
- Ventanas emergentes constantes, incluso fuera de los botones.
- Mensajes urgentes como “su teléfono está infectado” o “actualice ahora”.
- Promesas de “HD garantizado”, “sin anuncios” o “sin cortes”.
- Solicitud de tarjeta bancaria, contraseña o permisos del sistema.
Si una página saturada de anuncios y solicitudes de información presume de ser “gratis”, esa es su verdadera trampa: monetiza cada dato que entregas y cada clic que hagas.
PUBLICIDAD
Ver partidos como Nacional vs. Fortaleza en sitios no oficiales puede salir mucho más caro de lo que parece. Las plataformas legítimas, aunque requieran suscripción o pago puntual, ofrecen garantías de calidad, privacidad y seguridad digital. La prevención y la elección de servicios autorizados son la mejor defensa frente a las amenazas ocultas del streaming ilegal. Proteger tus datos y dispositivos debe ser tan prioritario como disfrutar del fútbol en vivo.

articles.title: Can't decide between buying a Chromebook now or waiting for a Googlebook? Here are the key differences you need to know about
articles.text:
Should you buy a Chromebook now or wait for the Googlebook?
Chrome vs Google — the battle of the books
Google has barely uttered a word about its forthcoming Googlebook since its big reveal back in May, a state of affairs that doesn't inspire much confidence. It's almost as if the company has been trying to decide how best to deal with the negative reaction towards these incoming laptops, which have an OS that runs not just ChromeOS but also Android apps natively.
This silence has meant that many people have forgotten about the Googlebook. These devices weren't even mentioned at Computex 2026 (not directly, anyway) and I too had barely thought about them until leaks started popping up recently.
Now, at last, we've heard that Google is holding a press event in New York next month at which the media will be able to go hands-on with the new machines. However, this is not an official launch or announcement, and the full details of the Googlebook will be kept under wraps for a bit longer afterwards (as Chrome Unboxed reported earlier this week).
Still, it's clear that the full launch isn't too far off, and at any rate, we now know a bit more about these laptops thanks to all the recent leaks.
So, if you still find yourself wondering what the Googlebook is all about — and whether you should wait to buy one, rather than shelling out for a Chromebook right now – I can help. Read on to find out which laptop will be best suited to you, and how these devices fit together in Google's laptop landscape.
Chromebooks aren't going anywhere
Google made it clear right from the start that it isn't doing away with Chromebooks. These devices running ChromeOS will continue to be manufactured alongside Googlebooks, with the latter positioned as a higher-end offering.
This is a crucial factor to consider, because if you think that Googlebooks are going to be anything like affordable, this isn't the case. Google has said itself that these are 'premium' devices and that's a word which means one thing: they'll be pricey.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
How pricey? Well, that's obviously still up for debate, but the leaks have shown some notebooks that look distinctly expensive — and with rumored pricing above the $1,000 mark (in the US) thus far. These are just rumors, of course, but the broad expectation is that this will be the kind of price tag you're looking at with a Googlebook.
So, if you want a Chromebook because it's a wallet-friendly product, then buy one now without hesitation. Especially given that based on what's happening with the RAM crisis of late, all laptops are likely to get more expensive as 2026 rolls on; you'll probably save more than a few notes by buying sooner, rather than later.
Googlebook means more heavyweight performance
Premium doesn't just mean costly, of course. A high-end laptop will also be expected to perform admirably, to be well-built, and to look good.
We certainly expect Googlebooks to pack a good deal more performance punch than Chromebooks, and they're designed to run more heavyweight apps, such as Adobe Premiere Pro (as spotted in a leaked photo) — not something that's possible on a Chromebook.
You'll also be able to natively run Android apps on the Googlebook, which gives the device a lot of versatility. (Based on rumors, there's likely to be a 'handoff' style feature to work with your Android phone, too). Gemini and AI abilities are also set to feature in the Googlebook, so you'll be able to get a lot more done in that respect compared to on a Chromebook.
If you're more of a power-user — and keen to explore AI features (though it remains to be seen exactly what Google will pull off in this department) — the Googlebook will be more your kind of laptop. Everyday users who are just after a laptop to do basic computing tasks, such as browsing, emails, and watching videos, will be fine with a Chromebook.
Two-tier system
What Google is bringing in here is essentially two different tiers of laptops. The Chromebook will remain as the baseline offering, including a few more premium models that'll drain your wallet by a little more. The Googlebook, meanwhile, will sit right at the top of the tree, with higher price tags (that could potentially be a lot higher).
If you want a solid, everyday, more affordable laptop, just get a Chromebook now. There's no need to wait for the Googlebook, because it's not going to do much more for you relative to the far higher price you'll be paying.
If you want a premium piece of more performant hardware with a more flexible OS that runs Android apps and fully-fledged software such as the likes of Adobe Premiere Pro — and, crucially, if you're willing to pay for it, then by all means hold out for the Googlebook that's coming later this year.
That said, those of you who do wait may have to suffer the possible slings and arrows of being an early adopter: namely the kind of bugs and teething troubles that new operating systems often bring with them. Google has a lot going on here, considering that its new platform will be juggling two ecosystems, both desktop and mobile.
So, for those who are diving in at the deep end with a Googlebook right from the off, bear all that in mind, and remember that some Android apps in particular may be flakier until the platform finds itself a more solid footing in time.
I remain concerned that Google hasn't really sold this new laptop category very effectively yet, and I hope that changes when the NDAs lift after that press event next month, and we all start to get a full look at the capabilities of these devices. Watch this space.

articles.title: Windows 11 cambia para siempre el menú cuando das clic derecho en tu PC: estas son las nuevas opciones
articles.text:
Microsoft ha iniciado una transformación en el menú contextual que se despliega al dar clic derecho en Windows 11. Esta renovación busca responder a años de quejas de los usuarios por la lentitud y la falta de claridad.
Además, la empresa busca dar inicio a un etapacentrada en la personalización y la eficiencia para millones de personas que dependen de Windows en su trabajo diario, por lo que los cambios irán llegando de a poco.
PUBLICIDAD
Cuáles son los motivos por los que cambia el menú del clic derecho en Windows 11
El equipo de Microsoft identificó que los pequeños fallos cotidianos, como demoras al abrir el menú contextual o bloqueos inesperados al renombrar archivos, generaban gran frustración.
Estos problemas, aunque menores en apariencia, terminaban eclipsando la experiencia general del sistema operativo. Según la propia compañía, “lo que la gente más recuerda son los peores momentos”, como un menú de clic derecho que responde con lentitud o una vista de inicio que parpadea y se recarga inesperadamente.
PUBLICIDAD
Con el objetivo de atacar estos puntos críticos, los ingenieros de Microsoft analizaron en profundidad los factores que provocaban congelamientos y retrasos. Se eliminaron decenas de posibles cuellos de botella, logrando que tanto el Explorador de archivos como el menú contextual funcionen de manera más fluida y predecible.
La razón principal de esta renovación es clara: devolver al usuario el control y acelerar las tareas cotidianas. El menú contextual es una de las interacciones más frecuentes en Windows. Si no funciona bien, el flujo de trabajo puede verse afectado de inmediato.
PUBLICIDAD
El nuevo menú contextual de Windows 11 presenta una estructura que facilita el acceso a las funciones más utilizadas y elimina la sobrecarga visual que se fue acumulando con el tiempo. Con esto, la compañía busca que cada clic derecho sea rápido, intuitivo y adecuado a las necesidades particulares de cada persona.
Cuáles son los cambios que llegan a Windows 11
La actualización del menú contextual trae consigo varios cambios tangibles. El primero y más notorio es la velocidad de apertura: el menú ahora aparece casi de inmediato tras hacer clic derecho, eliminado la molesta espera que muchos usuarios experimentaban.
PUBLICIDAD
Esta mejora se logra gracias a una limpieza del menú principal y a la optimización del procesamiento interno, que antes se veía ralentizado por la cantidad de opciones añadidas por aplicaciones externas.
Otra novedad destacada es la personalización. En la parte inferior del nuevo menú contextual ahora aparece la opción “Personalizar menú”, que lleva directamente a una nueva sección en la aplicación de Configuración, bajo el apartado de Personalización.
PUBLICIDAD
Desde allí, cada usuario puede elegir qué comandos y extensiones de aplicaciones aparecen en el menú principal y cuáles quedan relegados a submenús. Por ejemplo, se puede decidir si las opciones de “Enviar a” o “Crear acceso directo” están activas o no, e incluso agregar comandos que antes no estaban disponibles, como “Imprimir”.
El usuario ahora tiene la capacidad de configurar el menú según sus hábitos y preferencias, adaptándolo a las rutinas adquiridas durante años de uso de versiones anteriores de Windows. Entre las opciones de personalización se incluye la posibilidad de mostrar los comandos principales — Cortar, Copiar, Pegar, Renombrar, Eliminar y Compartir — en formato de lista directamente en el menú, en lugar de dispersos en una fila de iconos.
PUBLICIDAD
Además, se puede mover la opción de Propiedades al final del menú, acercando la experiencia a lo que ofrecía Windows 10, para quienes prefieren esa disposición.
La actualización también simplifica la organización visual del menú: las acciones más habituales permanecen en la parte superior, mientras que las menos usadas pueden desplazarse a submenús, lo que reduce el desorden y facilita encontrar rápidamente la función buscada.

articles.title: Big companies are racing ahead on AI adoption for fear of being left behind
articles.text:
AI isn't killing jobs yet: Over 50% of businesses say AI is creating roles as massive upskilling push begins
AI is not killing jobs; it is creating more
- Over half (54%) of UK businesses say AI created new jobs, new study finds
- A similar amount (58%) plan to raise AI skills investment soon
- Some firms plan to spend up to £250,000 on Artificial Intelligence training
Concerns that AI would eliminate jobs have dominated public conversation for years, fueling fears of mass unemployment and disruption.
A report from the Lloyds Business Barometer claims over half (54%) of UK businesses say AI has already created new jobs within their organizations.
The findings arrive as firms increasingly treat AI adoption as central to competitiveness, workforce skills, and long-term business growth strategy.
Companies ramp up AI skills spending
The majority (58%) of businesses say they now plan to increase investment in AI tools and skill training over the next twelve months - and of the businesses planning to raise AI investment, 42% expect to spend between £25,000 and £100,000 during the coming year.
Another 26% expect to spend between £100,000 and £250,000, showing a clear appetite for deeper AI skills funding across sectors.
Despite this spending push, 31% of businesses admit their current workforce still lacks the AI skills the company actually needs.
To close that gap, 43% of firms are introducing formal AI skills training while 32% are expanding programs already in place.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
A smaller share, 24%, say they now prioritize AI skills when hiring, while 21% are creating entirely new AI-specific roles.
A widening gap between large and small firms
Overall, nearly two-thirds (61%) of UK firms say they currently use AI in some form, though adoption varies sharply by company size and reach.
Cost, cited by 18% of businesses, remains the most common barrier, followed closely by data quality and skills access at 17% each.
Domestic-only firms cite cost as their biggest barrier at 23%, while international firms point more often to data quality at 19%.
Larger businesses with annual turnover above £10 million report AI usage averaging 79%, far ahead of smaller and domestic-only competitors nationwide.
Nearly two-thirds of larger firms say their current workforce already possesses the AI skills the business truly needs right now.
Among larger firms already using AI, 74% cite productivity gains as their main reason for continued and future investment decisions.
Nearly six in 10 businesses believe companies that fail to adopt AI risk falling behind their competitors within a few years, but this confidence in AI's competitive importance varies by size, with 73% of large firms agreeing compared with 54% of the smallest firms.
"AI has the potential to be as transformative for businesses as the internet was," said Amanda Murphy, CEO of Lloyds Business and Commercial Banking.
Murphy added that success depends far more on building internal skills, culture, and confidence than on simply purchasing new technology.
The figures suggest AI adoption across the UK economy is accelerating faster than the workforce skills needed to sustain it.
Whether businesses can close that widening skills gap quickly enough may determine which companies gain a lasting competitive advantage overall.
